title: How smartphones stay cool: Exploring phase change in Ultra-Thin Vapor Chambers
subtitle: A sealed 0.35 mm copper pouch uses a few drops of boiling water and a copper-powder wick to move heat 20x faster than solid metal—keeping an 80W phone chip from throttling.
subject: Thermal
summary: A plain-English engineering look at 0.35 mm smartphone vapor chambers: why solid copper hits a wall, how copper powder pumps water without moving parts, and why trapped gas ruins cooling over time.

## 1. Why Solid Copper Isn't Fast Enough {{ FIGURE_0 }} Modern smartphone chips have a heat problem. A flagship processor packs billions of 3nm transistors into a square of silicon barely $10 \times 10 \text{ mm}$ across—about the size of your pinky fingernail. During heavy 3D gaming or 4K video recording, that tiny square can pump out heat fluxes past **80 W/cm²**. If you try to spread that heat using a flat sheet of solid copper or graphite, you run straight into Fourier's law of heat conduction: $$q = -k \cdot A \cdot \nabla T$$ Here, $k$ is the material's thermal conductivity and $A$ is the cross-sectional area the heat has to travel through. Solid copper is a great conductor ($k \approx 390 \text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$), but inside a thin phone, the cooling sheet has to be thinner than **0.40 mm**. Because that cross-sectional area $A$ is razor-thin, heat gets bottlenecked right over the processor. Within seconds, the chip spikes past $105^\circ\text{C}$ and throttles its clock speed to keep from melting.

### How Boiling Beats Solid Metal An ultra-thin vapor chamber gets around copper's bottleneck by **boiling and condensing water** inside a flat, vacuum-sealed copper pouch. Instead of waiting for heat to slowly vibrate from one copper atom to the next, the chamber uses the heat from the chip to turn a tiny drop of purified water into steam: $$q = \dot{m} \cdot h_{fg}$$ Water is the secret weapon here because its **latent heat of vaporization** ($h_{fg}$) is huge—it takes a massive amount of heat energy just to turn liquid water into vapor without even raising its temperature: $$h_{fg} \approx 2.45 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg} \quad (\text{at } 40^\circ\text{C})$$ Because the inside of the copper pouch is pumped down to a near-vacuum, the water boils at just $35^\circ\text{C}$ to $45^\circ\text{C}$. As soon as the chip warms up, water right above it flashes into steam and shoots outward toward the cooler edges of the phone at high speed. When the steam touches the cooler walls, it condenses back into liquid water, dumping its heat evenly across the whole frame of the phone. By moving heat with fast-moving steam instead of solid metal, a **0.35 mm** vapor chamber acts like a material with an effective thermal conductivity of: $$k_{\text{eff}} > 6{,}500 - 10{,}000 \text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$$ In plain English, that is **16 to 25 times faster at spreading heat than a solid sheet of pure copper** of the exact same size. ## 2. Moving Water Without a Pump: How the Copper Wick Works Once the steam reaches the cool edges of the phone and turns back into water droplets, how does that water get back to the hot processor—even when you hold your phone upside down? There is no mechanical pump inside. Instead, the inner walls are lined with a porous copper **wick** that acts like a stiff metal sponge. For the loop to keep running without boiling dry, the wick's capillary suction has to beat all the friction slowing the water and steam down: $$\Delta P_{\text{capillary, max}} \ge \Delta P_{\text{liquid}} + \Delta P_{\text{vapor}} + \Delta P_{\text{gravity}}$$
Why Flat Vapor Chambers Beat Squashed Heat Pipes in Phones

Why not just flatten a normal round laptop heat pipe?

  • The Cube-Law Choke ($\Delta P_{\text{vapor}} \propto 1/h^3$): When you squash a round tube below 0.8 mm, its center pinches down into two tiny side tunnels, spiking steam drag by over 30x. A flat vapor chamber keeps a wide, open 2D runway for steam.
  • 360° Heat Spreading: A heat pipe only carries heat in a 1D line. A vapor chamber spreads heat outward in all directions at once, avoiding hot stripes on the motherboard.
  • Direct Contact: The flat pouch sits directly against the chip shield and frame, cutting out extra glue layers and dropping thermal resistance by $0.12 \text{ K/W}$.
{{ FIGURE_1 }} ### How Pore Size Creates Suction The suction inside the copper sponge comes from surface tension—the same physics that pulls coffee up into the edge of a paper napkin. It follows the equation: $$\Delta P_c = \frac{2 \cdot \sigma \cdot \cos \theta}{r_{\text{pore}}}$$ Here, $\sigma$ is water's surface tension ($\approx 0.072 \text{ N/m}$), $\theta$ is the wetting angle on clean copper ($\approx 0^\circ$), and $r_{\text{pore}}$ is the radius of the tiny gaps between copper grains. Notice that $r_{\text{pore}}$ is on the bottom of the fraction: **the smaller the pores, the stronger the suction**. Pores just $20 \,\mu\text{m}$ wide create over $7{,}200 \text{ Pa}$ of suction—more than enough to pull water straight uphill against gravity. ### The 0.35 mm Squeeze: Why Steam Drag Explodes Making a vapor chamber just **0.35 mm** thick—about the thickness of four sheets of printer paper—creates a nasty fluid-flow problem. Out of that $0.35 \text{ mm}$ total height, the top and bottom copper sheets take up $0.08 \text{ mm}$ each, and the copper wick layers take up another $0.06 \text{ mm}$ each. That leaves an empty middle gap for the steam that is barely: $$h_{\text{vapor}} \approx 0.35 - (2 \times 0.08) - (2 \times 0.06) \approx 0.07 \text{ to } 0.11 \text{ mm} \quad (70 - 110 \,\mu\text{m})$$ When gas flows between two flat plates, friction follows the Hagen-Poiseuille law—meaning pressure drop scales with the **cube** of the gap height: $$\Delta P_{\text{vapor}} = \frac{12 \cdot \mu_v \cdot \dot{m} \cdot L}{\rho_v \cdot w \cdot h_{\text{vapor}}^3}$$ In plain terms: shrinking the steam gap from $0.30 \text{ mm}$ down to $0.09 \text{ mm}$ doesn't just make friction $3\times$ worse—it multiplies steam drag by **37 times**: $$\left(\frac{0.30}{0.09}\right)^3 \approx 37\times$$ Under heavy loads ($>50\text{ W}$), steam has to whip through that microscopic gap so fast that it approaches the . If steam drag gets too high, water can't circulate back to the chip and the chamber dries out. ## 3. Keeping a 0.35 mm Vacuum Shell From Crushing Under Air Pressure Building a paper-thin hollow copper pouch is tougher than it looks. A typical smartphone vapor chamber is about $120 \times 65 \text{ mm}$, giving it a surface area of $78 \text{ cm}^2$. Because all the air inside is pumped out to a deep vacuum ($10^{-3} \text{ Torr}$), normal outside air pressure ($101.3 \text{ kPa}$) is constantly trying to squash the pouch flat. Across the face of the chamber, that adds up to a crushing force of: $$F_{\text{atm}} = P \cdot A = (101{,}325 \text{ Pa}) \cdot (0.0078 \text{ m}^2) \approx 790 \text{ N} \quad (\approx 80.5 \text{ kgf})$$ That's the weight of a **177-pound person standing directly on top of a hollow copper foil only 0.08 mm thick**. Without internal support columns holding the roof up, outside air would instantly flatten the chamber and pinch the steam gap shut. {{ FIGURE_2 }} Instead of welding hundreds of tiny loose posts, factories use acid photo-etching to carve away half the thickness of a solid copper sheet—leaving behind a grid of built-in copper pillars that hold up 80 kgf of air pressure. Fine spherical copper powder (35–55 μm wide) is spread across the etched floor and baked at 850°C. A stream of hydrogen gas strips away tarnish so the powder grains fuse into a clean, water-loving sponge. The top and bottom copper sheets are clamped together and sealed around the edges with a pinpoint fiber laser. The weld must be completely airtight, with helium leak rates below 10^-9 mbar·L/s. Air is sucked out through a tiny copper tail-pipe, a few drops of ultra-pure degassed water are injected, and an ultrasonic press cold-welds the pipe shut. ### Turning Loose Copper Dust Into a Solid Sponge Thick laptop heat pipes often use woven copper wire mesh, but wire mesh is too bulky for a $0.35 \text{ mm}$ phone chamber. Instead, smartphone chambers use **sintered copper powder**. Tiny copper spheres ($35 \text{ to } 55 \,\mu\text{m}$ wide—finer than table salt) are dusted onto the copper sheet and run through a furnace at $850^\circ\text{C}$. That temperature is hot enough (about $78\%$ of copper's melting point) that the copper atoms where two spheres touch fuse together into solid necks without melting the spheres flat. The result is a rigid, three-dimensional copper sponge with $42\% \text{ to } 48\%$ open space inside—giving water thousands of connected micro-tunnels to travel through. ## 4. The Wick Tradeoff: Fine Powder vs. Fast Flow When engineers design the copper sponge inside a vapor chamber, they face a classic tug-of-war between **suction strength** and **water flow speed**.

 ### Why One Powder Size Isn't Enough How easily water moves through the copper sponge is governed by : $$\Delta P_{\text{liquid}} = \frac{\mu_l \cdot \dot{m} \cdot L}{\rho_l \cdot A_w \cdot K}$$ Here, $K$ is the wick's **permeability**—a measure of how open the pathways are. For packed spherical powder, permeability follows the Kozeny-Carman formula: $$K = \frac{\epsilon^3 \cdot d_{\text{powder}}^2}{150 \cdot (1 - \epsilon)^2}$$ Where $\epsilon$ is the percentage of open pore space and $d_{\text{powder}}$ is the diameter of the copper grains. Here is the catch: - To get **strong suction** ($\Delta P_c \propto 1/r_{\text{pore}}$), you want **tiny powder grains** ($< 20 \,\mu\text{m}$). - But water flow ease scales with the **square of grain size** ($K \propto d_{\text{powder}}^2$). Cutting the powder size in half chokes water flow by **$4\times$**, starving the chip of water. To get around this, modern phone chambers use a **two-layer** () wick. The bottom layer against the copper wall uses coarser $60 \,\mu\text{m}$ grains to form a low-drag highway for returning water ($K > 2.5 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}^2$). Right on top of that sits a thin cap of ultra-fine $25 \,\mu\text{m}$ powder or 400-mesh copper screen. The fine top layer provides strong suction where the water boils, while the coarse bottom layer lets water cruise back from the edges with minimal friction. ## 5. How Vapor Chambers Fail: Dry-Out, Choking, and Trapped Gas A vapor chamber has no moving parts to wear out, but three physical limits can still cause it to fail inside a phone: ### 1. Boiling Dry Over the Chip (Evaporator Dry-Out) When you run a heavy game or export 4K video in the summer sun, heat density over the processor can push past the chamber's . Water boils away faster than the copper sponge can pull fresh liquid back in. Once the sponge directly over the chip dries out, a blanket of steam insulates the copper wall. Without boiling water to carry heat away, chip temperatures shoot up by **$25^\circ\text{C}$ to $35^\circ\text{C}$ in less than a second**, forcing an instant thermal throttle. ### 2. Steam Traffic Jams (Sonic Choking) Because the chamber is under vacuum, water vapor inside has very low density (at $40^\circ\text{C}$, steam is nearly $20{,}000\times$ less dense than liquid water). To carry significant heat, that thin steam has to race down the $0.09 \text{ mm}$ gap at huge speeds. The maximum heat it can carry before hitting the speed of sound ($c_{\text{sonic}} \approx 430 \text{ m/s}$) is: $$q_{\text{sonic}} = A_v \cdot \rho_v \cdot h_{fg} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\gamma \cdot R \cdot T}{2(\gamma + 1)}}$$ When a phone is cold (below $20^\circ\text{C}$), steam density drops even lower, making it easy for expanding vapor to hit a sonic bottleneck right as it leaves the chip—temporarily capping heat transfer until the chamber warms up. ### 3. The Slow Killer: Trapped Hydrogen Gas (NCG) The biggest threat over a phone's 4-to-5-year lifespan is . Even in a clean vacuum, any leftover trace of copper tarnish ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$) or cleaning oil slowly reacts with warm water to release hydrogen gas: $$\text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \uparrow$$ Unlike steam, hydrogen gas **never condenses back into liquid** at phone temperatures. Flowing steam sweeps those hydrogen molecules into the far corners of the vapor chamber and traps them there like an air bubble in a radiator. Just $0.005 \text{ cm}^3$ of trapped hydrogen can blanket $30\%$ of the chamber's cooling surface, making a 3-year-old phone run noticeably hotter than it did on day one. To prevent this, top factories bake and chemically passivate every chamber for 72 hours before sealing it. ## 6. Testing on the Bench: Thermal Cameras and Gravity Checks Before a vapor chamber design is cleared for mass production, engineers put samples through a brutal set of bench tests. {{ FIGURE_3 }} ### Watching Heat Spread at 120 Frames per Second Bare copper is shiny and reflects infrared light like a mirror, which fools thermal cameras. To get true readings, engineers spray test chambers with a flat matte-black paint ($\epsilon = 0.95$) and clamp a $12 \times 12 \text{ mm}$ copper heater block onto the chip spot to simulate loads from $10\text{ W}$ up to $85\text{ W}$. A high-speed FLIR thermal camera films the surface at 120 frames per second to check three things: - **Even Heat Spreading:** A healthy vapor chamber lights up evenly across its whole surface. Under a steady $20\text{ W}$ load, the temperature gap between the hot chip spot and the far edge ($\Delta T_{\text{evap-cond}}$) must stay under **$3.5^\circ\text{C}$**. - **Low Thermal Resistance:** Total end-to-end thermal resistance must beat: $$R_{\text{th}} = \frac{T_{\text{hotspot}} - T_{\text{condenser}}}{Q} \le 0.08 \text{ K/W}$$ - **Upside-Down Gravity Test:** A phone has to cool just as well when held upright taking a photo as it does flat on a desk. Engineers spin the test rig through a full $360^\circ$ circle. Even when water has to climb $120 \text{ mm}$ straight uphill against gravity ($\Delta P_g = \rho g L \approx 1{,}168 \text{ Pa}$), the copper-powder wick must keep thermal resistance within $5\%$. By combining acid-etched support pillars, dual-layer sintered copper powder, and laser-welded vacuum seals, a **0.35 mm** pouch of water lets a pocket-sized phone run chip workloads that used to require a noisy metal heatsink and fan.

young_laplace.title: Young-Laplace Capillary Suction
young_laplace.body: When water sits inside a tiny copper pore, surface tension pulls the water surface into a curved meniscus. The smaller the pore, the stronger the suction pulling water back toward the hot chip—no mechanical pump required.

darcy_permeability.title: Darcy's Law & Wick Permeability
darcy_permeability.body: Darcy's law measures how easily water flows through a bed of packed copper powder. Larger powder grains leave bigger gaps ($K \propto d^2$), letting water flow with less friction—but sacrificing suction strength.

sonic_choking.title: The Sonic Choking Limit
sonic_choking.body: Because the inside of a vapor chamber is a near-vacuum, steam expands to a low density and shoots across the gap at high speed. If the steam hits the speed of sound ($\approx 430\text{ m/s}$), traffic jams and heat transfer hits a ceiling.

ncg_degradation.title: Non-Condensable Gas (NCG) Buildup
ncg_degradation.body: Over years of heating and cooling, trace copper oxides react with water to release tiny amounts of hydrogen gas ($\text{H}_2$). Because hydrogen won't condense back into liquid, steam pushes it into the corners of the chamber, blocking off cooling area.

critical_heat_flux.title: Critical Heat Flux (CHF) & Dry-Out
critical_heat_flux.body: If the processor dumps heat faster than the copper wick can pull fresh water back, the spot right over the chip boils completely dry. A pocket of steam blocks liquid from touching the copper, and chip temperatures jump 25°C in less than a second.

biporous_wick.title: Biporous (Dual-Layer) Copper Wick
biporous_wick.body: A two-layer wick gives engineers the best of both worlds: a base layer of coarse copper powder acts like a multi-lane highway for water return, while a top layer of fine powder provides strong capillary suction right over the chip.

sections.heading: 1. Why Solid Copper Isn't Fast Enough
sections.content:
{{ FIGURE_0 }} Modern smartphone chips have a heat problem. A flagship processor packs billions of 3nm transistors into a square of silicon barely $10 \times 10 \text{ mm}$ across—about the size of your pinky fingernail. During heavy 3D gaming or 4K video recording, that tiny square can pump out heat fluxes past **80 W/cm²**. If you try to spread that heat using a flat sheet of solid copper or graphite, you run straight into Fourier's law of heat conduction: $$q = -k \cdot A \cdot \nabla T$$ Here, $k$ is the material's thermal conductivity and $A$ is the cross-sectional area the heat has to travel through. Solid copper is a great conductor ($k \approx 390 \text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$), but inside a thin phone, the cooling sheet has to be thinner than **0.40 mm**. Because that cross-sectional area $A$ is razor-thin, heat gets bottlenecked right over the processor. Within seconds, the chip spikes past $105^\circ\text{C}$ and throttles its clock speed to keep from melting.

### How Boiling Beats Solid Metal An ultra-thin vapor chamber gets around copper's bottleneck by **boiling and condensing water** inside a flat, vacuum-sealed copper pouch. Instead of waiting for heat to slowly vibrate from one copper atom to the next, the chamber uses the heat from the chip to turn a tiny drop of purified water into steam: $$q = \dot{m} \cdot h_{fg}$$ Water is the secret weapon here because its **latent heat of vaporization** ($h_{fg}$) is huge—it takes a massive amount of heat energy just to turn liquid water into vapor without even raising its temperature: $$h_{fg} \approx 2.45 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg} \quad (\text{at } 40^\circ\text{C})$$ Because the inside of the copper pouch is pumped down to a near-vacuum, the water boils at just $35^\circ\text{C}$ to $45^\circ\text{C}$. As soon as the chip warms up, water right above it flashes into steam and shoots outward toward the cooler edges of the phone at high speed. When the steam touches the cooler walls, it condenses back into liquid water, dumping its heat evenly across the whole frame of the phone. By moving heat with fast-moving steam instead of solid metal, a **0.35 mm** vapor chamber acts like a material with an effective thermal conductivity of: $$k_{\text{eff}} > 6{,}500 - 10{,}000 \text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$$ In plain English, that is **16 to 25 times faster at spreading heat than a solid sheet of pure copper** of the exact same size.

sections.heading: 2. Moving Water Without a Pump: How the Copper Wick Works
sections.content:
Once the steam reaches the cool edges of the phone and turns back into water droplets, how does that water get back to the hot processor—even when you hold your phone upside down? There is no mechanical pump inside. Instead, the inner walls are lined with a porous copper **wick** that acts like a stiff metal sponge. For the loop to keep running without boiling dry, the wick's capillary suction has to beat all the friction slowing the water and steam down: $$\Delta P_{\text{capillary, max}} \ge \Delta P_{\text{liquid}} + \Delta P_{\text{vapor}} + \Delta P_{\text{gravity}}$$
Why Flat Vapor Chambers Beat Squashed Heat Pipes in Phones

Why not just flatten a normal round laptop heat pipe?

  • The Cube-Law Choke ($\Delta P_{\text{vapor}} \propto 1/h^3$): When you squash a round tube below 0.8 mm, its center pinches down into two tiny side tunnels, spiking steam drag by over 30x. A flat vapor chamber keeps a wide, open 2D runway for steam.
  • 360° Heat Spreading: A heat pipe only carries heat in a 1D line. A vapor chamber spreads heat outward in all directions at once, avoiding hot stripes on the motherboard.
  • Direct Contact: The flat pouch sits directly against the chip shield and frame, cutting out extra glue layers and dropping thermal resistance by $0.12 \text{ K/W}$.
{{ FIGURE_1 }} ### How Pore Size Creates Suction The suction inside the copper sponge comes from surface tension—the same physics that pulls coffee up into the edge of a paper napkin. It follows the equation: $$\Delta P_c = \frac{2 \cdot \sigma \cdot \cos \theta}{r_{\text{pore}}}$$ Here, $\sigma$ is water's surface tension ($\approx 0.072 \text{ N/m}$), $\theta$ is the wetting angle on clean copper ($\approx 0^\circ$), and $r_{\text{pore}}$ is the radius of the tiny gaps between copper grains. Notice that $r_{\text{pore}}$ is on the bottom of the fraction: **the smaller the pores, the stronger the suction**. Pores just $20 \,\mu\text{m}$ wide create over $7{,}200 \text{ Pa}$ of suction—more than enough to pull water straight uphill against gravity. ### The 0.35 mm Squeeze: Why Steam Drag Explodes Making a vapor chamber just **0.35 mm** thick—about the thickness of four sheets of printer paper—creates a nasty fluid-flow problem. Out of that $0.35 \text{ mm}$ total height, the top and bottom copper sheets take up $0.08 \text{ mm}$ each, and the copper wick layers take up another $0.06 \text{ mm}$ each. That leaves an empty middle gap for the steam that is barely: $$h_{\text{vapor}} \approx 0.35 - (2 \times 0.08) - (2 \times 0.06) \approx 0.07 \text{ to } 0.11 \text{ mm} \quad (70 - 110 \,\mu\text{m})$$ When gas flows between two flat plates, friction follows the Hagen-Poiseuille law—meaning pressure drop scales with the **cube** of the gap height: $$\Delta P_{\text{vapor}} = \frac{12 \cdot \mu_v \cdot \dot{m} \cdot L}{\rho_v \cdot w \cdot h_{\text{vapor}}^3}$$ In plain terms: shrinking the steam gap from $0.30 \text{ mm}$ down to $0.09 \text{ mm}$ doesn't just make friction $3\times$ worse—it multiplies steam drag by **37 times**: $$\left(\frac{0.30}{0.09}\right)^3 \approx 37\times$$ Under heavy loads ($>50\text{ W}$), steam has to whip through that microscopic gap so fast that it approaches the . If steam drag gets too high, water can't circulate back to the chip and the chamber dries out.

sections.heading: 3. Keeping a 0.35 mm Vacuum Shell From Crushing Under Air Pressure
sections.content:
Building a paper-thin hollow copper pouch is tougher than it looks. A typical smartphone vapor chamber is about $120 \times 65 \text{ mm}$, giving it a surface area of $78 \text{ cm}^2$.

Because all the air inside is pumped out to a deep vacuum ($10^{-3} \text{ Torr}$), normal outside air pressure ($101.3 \text{ kPa}$) is constantly trying to squash the pouch flat. Across the face of the chamber, that adds up to a crushing force of:

$$F_{\text{atm}} = P \cdot A = (101{,}325 \text{ Pa}) \cdot (0.0078 \text{ m}^2) \approx 790 \text{ N} \quad (\approx 80.5 \text{ kgf})$$

That's the weight of a **177-pound person standing directly on top of a hollow copper foil only 0.08 mm thick**. Without internal support columns holding the roof up, outside air would instantly flatten the chamber and pinch the steam gap shut.

### Turning Loose Copper Dust Into a Solid Sponge

Thick laptop heat pipes often use woven copper wire mesh, but wire mesh is too bulky for a $0.35 \text{ mm}$ phone chamber. Instead, smartphone chambers use **sintered copper powder**. Tiny copper spheres ($35 \text{ to } 55 \,\mu\text{m}$ wide—finer than table salt) are dusted onto the copper sheet and run through a furnace at $850^\circ\text{C}$.

That temperature is hot enough (about $78\%$ of copper's melting point) that the copper atoms where two spheres touch fuse together into solid necks without melting the spheres flat. The result is a rigid, three-dimensional copper sponge with $42\% \text{ to } 48\%$ open space inside—giving water thousands of connected micro-tunnels to travel through.

sections.heading: 4. The Wick Tradeoff: Fine Powder vs. Fast Flow
sections.content:
When engineers design the copper sponge inside a vapor chamber, they face a classic tug-of-war between **suction strength** and **water flow speed**.

 ### Why One Powder Size Isn't Enough How easily water moves through the copper sponge is governed by : $$\Delta P_{\text{liquid}} = \frac{\mu_l \cdot \dot{m} \cdot L}{\rho_l \cdot A_w \cdot K}$$ Here, $K$ is the wick's **permeability**—a measure of how open the pathways are. For packed spherical powder, permeability follows the Kozeny-Carman formula: $$K = \frac{\epsilon^3 \cdot d_{\text{powder}}^2}{150 \cdot (1 - \epsilon)^2}$$ Where $\epsilon$ is the percentage of open pore space and $d_{\text{powder}}$ is the diameter of the copper grains. Here is the catch: - To get **strong suction** ($\Delta P_c \propto 1/r_{\text{pore}}$), you want **tiny powder grains** ($< 20 \,\mu\text{m}$). - But water flow ease scales with the **square of grain size** ($K \propto d_{\text{powder}}^2$). Cutting the powder size in half chokes water flow by **$4\times$**, starving the chip of water. To get around this, modern phone chambers use a **two-layer** () wick. The bottom layer against the copper wall uses coarser $60 \,\mu\text{m}$ grains to form a low-drag highway for returning water ($K > 2.5 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}^2$). Right on top of that sits a thin cap of ultra-fine $25 \,\mu\text{m}$ powder or 400-mesh copper screen. The fine top layer provides strong suction where the water boils, while the coarse bottom layer lets water cruise back from the edges with minimal friction.

sections.heading: 5. How Vapor Chambers Fail: Dry-Out, Choking, and Trapped Gas
sections.content:
A vapor chamber has no moving parts to wear out, but three physical limits can still cause it to fail inside a phone:

### 1. Boiling Dry Over the Chip (Evaporator Dry-Out)

When you run a heavy game or export 4K video in the summer sun, heat density over the processor can push past the chamber's <TechnicalTangent term="Critical Heat Flux" category="PHASE CHANGE // DRY-OUT" definition="If the processor dumps heat faster than the copper wick can pull fresh water back, the spot right over the chip boils completely dry. A pocket of steam blocks liquid from touching the copper, and chip temperatures jump 25°C in less than a second." equation="q_{\text{CHF}} \approx 0.149 \rho_v^{1/2} h_{fg} [\sigma g (\rho_l - \rho_v)]^{1/4}" />. Water boils away faster than the copper sponge can pull fresh liquid back in. Once the sponge directly over the chip dries out, a blanket of steam insulates the copper wall. Without boiling water to carry heat away, chip temperatures shoot up by **$25^\circ\text{C}$ to $35^\circ\text{C}$ in less than a second**, forcing an instant thermal throttle.

### 2. Steam Traffic Jams (Sonic Choking)

Because the chamber is under vacuum, water vapor inside has very low density (at $40^\circ\text{C}$, steam is nearly $20{,}000\times$ less dense than liquid water). To carry significant heat, that thin steam has to race down the $0.09 \text{ mm}$ gap at huge speeds. The maximum heat it can carry before hitting the speed of sound ($c_{\text{sonic}} \approx 430 \text{ m/s}$) is:

$$q_{\text{sonic}} = A_v \cdot \rho_v \cdot h_{fg} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\gamma \cdot R \cdot T}{2(\gamma + 1)}}$$

When a phone is cold (below $20^\circ\text{C}$), steam density drops even lower, making it easy for expanding vapor to hit a sonic bottleneck right as it leaves the chip—temporarily capping heat transfer until the chamber warms up.

### 3. The Slow Killer: Trapped Hydrogen Gas (NCG)

The biggest threat over a phone's 4-to-5-year lifespan is <TechnicalTangent term="Non-Condensable Gas (NCG)" category="RELIABILITY // TRAPPED GAS" definition="Over years of heating and cooling, trace copper oxides react with water to release tiny amounts of hydrogen gas (H2). Because hydrogen won't condense back into liquid, steam pushes it into the corners of the chamber, blocking off cooling area." equation="\text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \uparrow" />.

Even in a clean vacuum, any leftover trace of copper tarnish ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$) or cleaning oil slowly reacts with warm water to release hydrogen gas:

$$\text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \uparrow$$

Unlike steam, hydrogen gas **never condenses back into liquid** at phone temperatures. Flowing steam sweeps those hydrogen molecules into the far corners of the vapor chamber and traps them there like an air bubble in a radiator. Just $0.005 \text{ cm}^3$ of trapped hydrogen can blanket $30\%$ of the chamber's cooling surface, making a 3-year-old phone run noticeably hotter than it did on day one. To prevent this, top factories bake and chemically passivate every chamber for 72 hours before sealing it.

sections.heading: 6. Testing on the Bench: Thermal Cameras and Gravity Checks
sections.content:
Before a vapor chamber design is cleared for mass production, engineers put samples through a brutal set of bench tests. {{ FIGURE_3 }} ### Watching Heat Spread at 120 Frames per Second Bare copper is shiny and reflects infrared light like a mirror, which fools thermal cameras. To get true readings, engineers spray test chambers with a flat matte-black paint ($\epsilon = 0.95$) and clamp a $12 \times 12 \text{ mm}$ copper heater block onto the chip spot to simulate loads from $10\text{ W}$ up to $85\text{ W}$. A high-speed FLIR thermal camera films the surface at 120 frames per second to check three things: - **Even Heat Spreading:** A healthy vapor chamber lights up evenly across its whole surface. Under a steady $20\text{ W}$ load, the temperature gap between the hot chip spot and the far edge ($\Delta T_{\text{evap-cond}}$) must stay under **$3.5^\circ\text{C}$**. - **Low Thermal Resistance:** Total end-to-end thermal resistance must beat: $$R_{\text{th}} = \frac{T_{\text{hotspot}} - T_{\text{condenser}}}{Q} \le 0.08 \text{ K/W}$$ - **Upside-Down Gravity Test:** A phone has to cool just as well when held upright taking a photo as it does flat on a desk. Engineers spin the test rig through a full $360^\circ$ circle. Even when water has to climb $120 \text{ mm}$ straight uphill against gravity ($\Delta P_g = \rho g L \approx 1{,}168 \text{ Pa}$), the copper-powder wick must keep thermal resistance within $5\%$. By combining acid-etched support pillars, dual-layer sintered copper powder, and laser-welded vacuum seals, a **0.35 mm** pouch of water lets a pocket-sized phone run chip workloads that used to require a noisy metal heatsink and fan.
